results.title: Data Reproducibility and other Data Lake Best Practices
results.content: In this article we share how to achieve Reproducible data with lakeFS, and dive into two specific examples for data lakes best practice:. ## How do I achieve Reproducible data with lakeFS? To make data reproducible, we recommend taking a new commit of your lakeFS repository every time the data in it changes. In a lakeFS repository, we are capable of taking many commits over the data, making many points in time reproducible. bash_command='lakectl commit lakefs://example_repo@example_dag_branch -m "extract data"',. For this reason, it makes sense to include lakeFS operations like branching and committing to a Kubeflow pipeline and achieve full experiment reproducibility. from kubernetes.client.models import V1EnvVar def commit_op(): return dsl.ContainerOp( name='commit', image='treeverse/lakectl', arguments=['commit', 'lakefs://example-repo/example-branch', '-m', 'commit message']) .add_env_variable(V1EnvVar(name='LAKECTL_CREDENTIALS_ACCESS_KEY_ID',value='AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE')) .add_env_variable(V1EnvVar(name='LAKECTL_CREDENTIALS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY',value='wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY')) .add_env_variable(V1EnvVar(name='LAKECTL_SERVER_ENDPOINT_URL',value='https://lakefs.example.com') ). Let’s put it all together, and create an example Kubeflow pipeline that implements a simple ETL workflow, and makes use of lakeFS operators to feature branch creation and commits. Thank you for reading how to create Reproducible data with lakeFS.

results.title: Pre-Commit & Git Hooks: Automate High Code Quality | Towards Data Science
results.content: # Pre-Commit & Git Hooks: Automate High Code Quality. How to improve your code quality with pre-commit and git hooks. ## What is Pre-Commit? Pre-commit is a Python package that makes creating pre-commit hooks much easier. It creates a hook for the `commit` command to automatically detect any issues in the code and makes creating the script seamless. It creates a configuration file to execute whenever the `git commit` command is called. One technique for ensuring robust deployment of machine learning models while adhering to good code quality is using git hooks and pre-commit. pip install pre-commit # pip poetry add pre-commit # I personally use poetry. This file will define what you want to run before committing your code. The first one is `pre-commit-hooks` repo that contains the hooks:. In this case, `id` is the specific and unique identifier for the exact pre-commit hook you want to run from the repo. After defining your file, you need to run `pre-commit install` to let pre-commit know you want to use pre-commit for this repo using the specified script. You should see the pre-commit hooks working. You can also see what your pre-commit is doing by running the following command `pre-commit run --all-files`. If you want to commit your code without running the hook, you can use `git commit --no-verify` to bypass it. I have pre-commit installed on my Medium-Articles repo, which we will use to showcase an example. repos: - repo: local hooks: - id: lint name: lint entry: make lint language: python types: [python] stages: [commit]. (medium-articles-py3.11) egorhowell@Egors-MBP Medium-Articles % git commit -m "testing pre-commit" [INFO] Initializing environment for local. You can fix this by running ``pip install "black[jupyter]"`` reformatted /Users/egorhowell/Repos/Medium-Articles/Data Science Basics/relu.py reformatted /Users/egorhowell/Repos/Medium-Articles/Time Series/Exponential Smoothing/holt_winters.py All done! Fixing /Users/egorhowell/Repos/Medium-Articles/Time Series/Exponential Smoothing/holt_winters.py Skipped 2 files make: Nothing to be done for `Data Science Basics/relu.py'. So, our pre-commit hook worked successfully! See below for some more pre-commit hooks examples. Pre-commit is a useful Python package that improves your git hook workflow and simplifies your scripts. As data scientists, we are becoming increasingly involved in model deployment, using technologies like git hooks and pre-commit to ensure our models reach production safely.

A pre-commit hook to check your Python dependencies against safety-db. It checks all files containing `requirements` in their name in the repo. Note that **telemetry data will be sent with every Safety call**. This includes the Python version, the Safety command used (check/license/review), and the Safety options used (without their values). repo revv1.4.2 hooks idpython-safety-dependencies-check. The first is the `files` argument. Simply put which file your dependencies are listed in. repo revv1.4.2 hooks idpython-safety-dependencies-check filespyproject.toml. repo revv1.4.2 hooks idpython-safety-dependencies-check args["--ignore=39153,39652"]. repo revv1.4.2 hooks idpython-safety-dependencies-check args["--groups=dev,test"]. By default, safety will use the `--full-report` flag so you can omit it for cleaner code. repo revv1.4.2 hooks idpython-safety-dependencies-check filespyproject.toml args["--short-report"]. You may for example want to use `always_run: true` in order to systematically run this hook, even when no dependency files have been modified. ## Supported files. `requirements` files are supported with any ending (e.g. .txt) and you can pass multiple files to be checked. `pyproject.toml` files are only supported with a single file per invocation. If you have subpackages with one `pyproject.toml` in each, you need to invoke the hook multiple times. Currently `poetry` is the only supported package manager for `pyproject.toml` files. When using a `pyproject.toml` file you need to have `poetry` in your `PATH`, and have at least version 1.2 installed, as well as `poetry-plugin-export`. A mix of both file types is not supported. results.content: The Stack v2 dataset is a collection of source code in over 600 programming languages. 3. The Stack v2 is a collection of source code from repositories with various licenses. * `bigcode/the-stack-v2`: the full "The Stack v2" dataset. * `bigcode/the-stack-v2-train-full-ids`: based on the `bigcode/the-stack-v2-dedup` dataset but further filtered with heuristics and spanning 600+ programming languages. * `bigcode/the-stack-v2-train-smol-ids`: based on the `bigcode/the-stack-v2-dedup` dataset but further filtered with heuristics and spanning 17 programming languages. **These datasets only contain the SWHIDs to download the code files and not the content of the files itself. The Stack v2 contains over 3B files in 600+ programming and markup languages. The dataset was created as part of the BigCode Project, an open scientific collaboration working on the responsible development of Large Language Models for Code (Code LLMs). The Stack serves as a pre-training dataset for Code LLMs, i.e., code-generating AI systems which enable the synthesis of programs from natural language descriptions as well as other from code snippets. # full dataset (file IDs only). ds = load_dataset("bigcode/the-stack-v2-train-full-ids", split="train"). ds = load_dataset("bigcode/the-stack-v2-train-full-ids", streaming=True, split="train"). ds = load_dataset("bigcode/the-stack-v2-train-full-ids", split="train", streaming=True). It is therefore difficult for other researchers to fully reproduce these models and understand what kind of pre-training data leads to high-performing code LLMs. By releasing an open large-scale code dataset we hope to make training of code LLMs more reproducible. 3.28B unique files belonging to 104.2M github repositories were collected by traversing the Software Heritage 2023-09-06 graph dataset. **Training Datasets**: For the training datasets the programming languages were filtered further to 17 and 600+ for the `the-stack-v2-smol-ids` and `the-stack-v2-full-ids` dataset, respecively. We extract repository-level license information from GH Archive for all repositories with matching names in the SWH dataset. The released dataset may contain sensitive information such as emails, IP addresses, and API/ssh keys that have previously been published to public repositories on GitHub. Deduplication has helped to reduce the amount of sensitive data that may exist. To the best of our knowledge, all files contained in the dataset are licensed with one of the permissive licenses (see list in Licensing information) or no license.
